title: Beyond Geometric Closure: Measuring and Diagnosing Mechanical Consistency in Visual Dynamics

paper.title: Beyond Geometric Closure: Measuring and Diagnosing Mechanical Consistency in Visual Dynamics
paper.abstract: Abstract Visual accuracy leaves open whether predicted motion obeys dynamics. We introduce a framework for measuring and diagnosing mechanical consistency in visual dynamics. An independent SI audit of rigid closed chains separates geometric admissibility, reaction-free actuator effort, and work–energy balance. Continuous scoring measures progress against fixed engineering targets, while reference replay quantifies measurement error. With three seeds per setting, we evaluate KeyCLD and CON across 343 planar assemblies at 64 / 256 64/256 pixels and V-JEPA + AC and LingBot-VA on 100 shared spatial test assemblies. CON reduces image MSE by 37.6 % / 37.2 % 37.6\%/37.2\% relative to persistence, yet neither planar model attains valid native geometry. At 256 pixels, calibrated RGB replay places forecast errors far above measurement error. With exact states, KeyCLD preserves geometry and RK4 training raises its score from 52.65 to 64.30. In both spatial pathways, CAD/IK reconstruction restores geometry while mean actuator residuals exceed five times the engineering targets. The interventions distinguish gains in visual prediction and geometric admissibility from remaining force and energy errors.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Picking objects, folding garments, and opening doors require predictions that support physical interaction. We study mechanical consistency: agreement between predicted motion and independently specified geometry, forces, and work in SI units. Evaluating these relations connects visual prediction to the actuator demands of physical interaction. Rigid closed chains make these relations concrete. Their closure constraints define admissible configurations, while speed and acceleration along the same path determine different actuator demands. A prediction can therefore trace a valid shape and still require the wrong torque, providing a controlled setting for diagnosing mechanical consistency. Our independent SI audit first checks the predicted configuration, then eliminates unknown joint reactions to evaluate actuator effort and work–energy balance ( Fig. 1 ). Reference replay and targeted interventions locate errors in coordinate readout, numerical integration, and the learned force model. Figure 1 : Four pathways from pixels to mechanics. (a) After reconstruction, blue/tan bars show measurable/unavailable fractions, with measurable/total counts and percentages. Effort/energy plots show cases, quartiles, ranges, and dashed tolerances. Below, six contributions sum to S comp S_{\rm comp} ; arrows show reconstruction gains and 50 marks the maximum kinematic contribution. Scores use task-specific targets with balanced seeds, families, and conditions; each spatial pathway contains 900 cases (LingBot FT: 50 updates). (b,c) Physical readouts feed kinematic and effort/energy tests using independent SI parameters ( B ​ u A = e 1 ​ τ A Bu_{A}=e_{1}\tau_{A} for planar chains). We apply the audit to constrained Lagrangian dynamics (KeyCLD) [ 4 ] and latent coupled oscillators (CON) [ 13 ] at two planar image resolutions, then to predictive features (V-JEPA 2.1 + AC) [ 12 , 1 ] and generative video–action modeling (LingBot-VA) [ 10 ] on Stewart and Delta mechanisms. Resolution and measurement controls test whether physical failures persist as visual information and localization accuracy improve. We contribute (1) a six-criterion framework for mechanical consistency and tracking, with continuous SI tolerance scoring; (2) reference calibration and interventions that separate observation, integration, and constitutive effects; and (3) a 343-assembly planar benchmark at two resolutions and a 100-test-assembly spatial study, spanning four modeling paradigms.

sections.heading: Structured mechanical learning.
sections.text: Hamiltonian [ 7 ] and Lagrangian networks [ 3 , 11 ] encode mechanical structure, while Cartesian constraints simplify admissible dynamics [ 5 ] . Analyses of these inductive biases [ 8 ] motivate testing what each structural choice guarantees. Our audit checks whether acceleration along the admissible manifold agrees with independently specified forces and work.

sections.heading: Learning physical evolution from images.
sections.text: Hamiltonian Generative Networks [ 15 ] and coordinate-aware Lagrangian models [ 17 ] link images to mechanics. KeyCLD learns constrained keypoints, masses, potential, and actuation [ 4 ] ; CON couples autoencoding to dissipative latent oscillators [ 13 ] . Dissipative SymODEN represents velocity-dependent forces [ 18 ] . V-JEPA 2.1 learns dense predictive features [ 12 ] for action-conditioned latent rollouts [ 1 ] ; LingBot-VA jointly models video and actions by autoregressive diffusion [ 10 ] . We audit their connections to SI states and forces.

sections.heading: Physical evaluation.
sections.text: Physion tests visual prediction [ 2 ] , MechVerse evaluates kinematic coupling [ 9 ] , and video benchmarks test physical laws [ 6 ] , including force–motion consistency in GAUGE [ 16 ] . We add closed-chain reaction elimination ( J ​ γ = 0 J\gamma=0 , J ​ N = 0 JN=0 ), SI force/work balance, and interventions on readout, training integration, and actuator response.

sections.heading: Calibrating the measurement path.
sections.text: Closure measures agreement with supplied rod lengths, whereas localization measures agreement with reference coordinates. A hard constraint can preserve the former even at 64 × 64 64\times 64 , so resolution changes the reader’s calibration rather than the engineering target. To measure the instrument’s contribution, we process reference and predicted RGB or features through the same frozen reader, reconstruction, and differentiator. Exact-state replay first isolates numerical error: quintic splines pass all six criteria on 54/54 planar reference trajectories. Correct-video replay then adds visual localization error, providing the reference against which forecast residuals are interpreted.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Design
sections.text: The experiments progress from visual resolution and coordinate anchoring on the 30 Hz planar corpus (Section 5 ), through constitutive response under 100 Hz torque excitation (Section 6 ), to predictive features and generated video under spatial position control (Section 7 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 Shared assembly corpus
sections.text: MuJoCo [ 14 ] trajectories rendered in Blender span 343 crank-rockers, offset sliders, and double-cranks with varied geometry and rigid-body properties ( Fig. 2 ). sections.heading: 5.1 Resolution intervention
sections.text: Under the → 256 64\!\to\!256 -pixel intervention, CON’s RGB gains over persistence remain 37.6 % / 37.2 % 37.6\%/37.2\% , with motion-region gains at both resolutions (Fig. 3 a,b). KeyCLD moves from near persistence to a 10.4 % 10.4\% mean RGB gain, and all 256-pixel forecasts are finite. Native geometry nevertheless fails in all four settings (Table 2 ): denser visual input, with the corresponding native capacity increase, does not establish a physical coordinate anchor. Continuous scores reveal which errors change. KeyCLD rises from 15.73 to 22.30 and CON from 7.23 to 10.96, mainly through velocity/acceleration consistency. Point scores remain below 1/100 at 256 pixels, and KeyCLD’s seed SD reaches 12.08. Thus the higher aggregate score describes differential consistency rather than accurate tracking.

sections.heading: A common RGB measurement path.
sections.text: On identical future frames, resolution-specific readers reduce correct-video Euclidean error from 2.13 to 0.334 mm, while 256-pixel forecast errors remain 195.0/208.5 mm for KeyCLD/CON. Passing correct and generated RGB through the same frozen phase path gives torque residuals of 0.116 versus 6.57/6.59 N m (Fig. 3 c). Reference energy error is 0.057 J, close to the 0.05 J target. The calibrated gap persists at 256 pixels, motivating state and force probes of its dynamical sources.

sections.heading: 5.2 What changes when the state is known?
sections.text: To separate perception from dynamics, the state controls replace image-derived coordinates and prefix velocities with their exact values. KeyCLD then preserves all geometric and differentiated constraints, making its force and energy residuals directly measurable. RK4 training reduces torque and energy residuals by more than 84 % 84\% ( Figs. 4 and 2 ) and raises S comp S_{\rm comp} from 52.65 to 64.30. The remaining energy failures show that this trajectory improvement stops short of matching the work supplied by the actuator. CON evolves six Cartesian coordinates padded to eight oscillator coordinates, so it must learn their curved one-dimensional admissible manifold. Its forecasts violate geometry, and RK4 increases native point error by 12.907 12.907 mm (95% interval [ 6.734 , 23.497 ] [6.734,23.497] ). Higher-order integration therefore has opposite effects on trajectory accuracy in the two pipelines. Figure 5 : Structural evidence. (a) Six checkpoints give zero odd torque on 648 states. The 100 Hz inset compares RMS odd acceleration (reference bars/dots, model crosses; symlog scale). (b) Each integrator pools 1,944 queries; the inset shows failed gain checks. (c) Mass fits use 44,280 poses, with separate/shared and family errors in the insets.

sections.heading: 5.3 Force and energy after a common geometric readout
sections.text: Using predicted crank direction and derivatives with public geometry, a causal post-hoc readout reconstructs admissible motion from each saved rollout. Large video corrections persist at both resolutions (Fig. 3 d), whereas exact-state KeyCLD needs less than a micrometer and CON’s state arms need 54.7 54.7 – 67.7 67.7 mm. Reconstruction raises 256-pixel S comp S_{\rm comp} to 53.10/48.26 for KeyCLD/CON by restoring geometric terms, while torque, energy, and point errors remain above target (Table 2 ). Matched traces (Fig. 4 g–i) show phase drift and above-target mechanical defects at both resolutions.

sections.heading: 6 Structural and Intervention Analysis
sections.text: Geometric reconstruction locates coordinate errors in both models. KeyCLD’s explicit torque interface additionally permits fixed-state force interventions, connecting its remaining mechanical errors to dissipation, actuator scale, and cross-assembly parameter sharing (Fig. 5 ).

sections.heading: 7 Predictive and Generative Spatial Dynamics
sections.text: Stewart and Delta mechanisms extend the audit to multiple actuators. Both spatial models use the same 50+50 test assemblies, three conditions, and seeds 42–44, forecasting 117 future frames at 30 Hz. V-JEPA freezes its encoder and trains the 24-layer AC predictor at 384 pixels for 3,000 exposures per family and seed, with decoded-state feedback. LingBot generates 256 × 256 256\times 256 RGB at 0/50 full-parameter updates (400 exposures per seed), giving 1,800 videos. sections.heading: 8 Implications and Conclusion
sections.text: Our framework measures mechanical consistency through independent SI criteria and diagnoses readout, integration, and constitutive errors through targeted interventions. KeyCLD’s exact-state controls demonstrate the value of explicit constraints and higher-order training integration. External geometry makes a distinct contribution: kinematics supplies 50.00 of KeyCLD 256’s 53.10 reconstructed points and 48.15 of adapted LingBot’s 53.12 (Fig. 1 ). Both retain force, energy, and tracking deficits against their respective engineering targets. These findings motivate combining visual learning with coordinate anchors, velocity-dependent dissipation, calibrated SI actuator response, and parameters conditioned on geometry and load.

sections.text: All models use fixed final-epoch checkpoints, with gradient updates and sequence exposures specifying the training budget across GPU and CPU environments. Maintaining the curved closure manifold then depends on the learned oscillator flow, and the observed forecasts depart from it despite exact-state supervision. Together with KeyCLD’s admissible state trajectories and residual force errors, these results locate complementary failures under the same physical criteria.

sections.heading: R.1 Data, representation, and training
sections.text: The spatial studies share 50 Stewart (H-A) and 50 Delta (H-B) test assemblies, each with three operating conditions, and use seeds 42, 43, and 44. The resulting 300-trajectory cohort is common to V-JEPA + AC and LingBot; each model retains its native training objective and budget. Assembly-level training/validation/test partitions are disjoint. Stewart has 14 training and four validation identities, while Delta has four of each. All five training views are used, giving 210 and 60 videos; validation and testing use the front view, giving 12 validation and 150 test trajectories per family. The assembly is the independent sampling unit. Each video contains 120 frames at 30 Hz, rendered at 640 × 640 640\times 640 and resized to 384 × 384 384\times 384 for V-JEPA’s encoder. The spatial model combines the released V-JEPA 2.1-B/16 encoder [ 12 ] with the AC predictor architecture [ 1 ] . The frozen encoder has 86.8 million parameters. Each observed frame forms a duplicated-frame tubelet, yielding 576 spatial tokens of width 768 without future-frame access. A separate 24-layer predictor, width 1024 with 16 heads, is initialized and trained for each family. Its inputs are visual features, standardized actuator position/velocity commands, and actuator state feedback. Training uses true training-state feedback; forecasting uses the model’s own decoded state. A physical readout pools encoder features to a 4 × 4 4\times 4 grid, concatenates 13 public camera-calibration values, and applies hidden layers of widths 512 and 256. Its outputs are the complete tree generalized position and velocity: 25/24 coordinates for Stewart and 22/21 for Delta. Training uses standardized state MSE for 60 epochs, AdamW with learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} and weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and batch size 256. Only the free-root quaternion is normalized. This seed-specific head supplies recurrent state feedback during forecasting; the independently calibrated heads below provide the common measurement interface. Their comparison holds the entire predicted feature trajectory fixed. The AC predictor uses eight-frame clips, teacher-forced feature L1 loss plus a two-step autoregressive L1 loss, and AdamW with weight decay 0.04 and maximum learning rate 4.25 × 10 − 4 4.25\times 10^{-4} . Each family and seed receives 3,000 sequence exposures with batch size eight and final-checkpoint forecasting: Stewart uses 386 updates over 15 epochs across 210 videos, with 60 exposures in the last epoch; Delta uses 400 updates over 50 epochs across 60 videos. The learning rate follows a cosine schedule fixed at initialization for the complete 15/50-epoch run, with warmup for the first 5% of epochs (at least one epoch). Parameters use float32 and forward arithmetic uses bfloat16 autocast. At test time, the model observes three RGB frames and predicts the remaining 117 at 30 Hz with a seven-frame autoregressive context, using public camera calibration and planned actuator commands. The audit measures this combined encoder, predictor, and physical-readout pathway. Because its outputs are discrete latent features, physical states are the common evaluation interface; RGB reconstruction and continuous-time ODE solvers belong to the other model pathways. sections.heading: Cohort and model.
sections.text: The generative study evaluates 50 Stewart and 50 Delta test assemblies. Each identity has low-speed, rated, and increased-load trajectories, giving 150 tests per family and 300 in total. Assembly identities are disjoint from the training and validation partitions; the three operating conditions remain grouped by identity. The same 210 Stewart and 60 Delta training videos cover five camera views, while testing uses the front view. We use the released LingBot-VA base model [ 10 ] , whose shared Transformer contains 5,088,872,670 parameters. Zero-shot generation uses the public base weights. Adaptation updates all Transformer parameters with the native joint video/action flow-matching objective, while freezing the VAE and text encoder. Each 120-frame training video is resized to 256 × 256 256\times 256 ; repeating its last frame gives 121 frames for VAE encoding into 31 latent frames.

sections.heading: Training and replication.
sections.text: Each of seeds 42, 43, and 44 starts independently from the pretrained weights and completes 50 updates. AdamW uses learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , β = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) \beta=(0.9,0.95) , weight decay 0.1, and ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} , with ten warmup updates. Microbatch size one and eight-step gradient accumulation give effective batch size eight and 400 sequence exposures per seed. Parameters and optimizer states use FP32, with BF16 forward arithmetic. sections.heading: Native causal generation and command interface.
sections.text: Each test uses the last image of the common three-frame prefix as LingBot’s single-image initialization. The remaining 117 frames are generated at 30 Hz and 256 × 256 256\times 256 using eight chunks of four latent frames, five video denoising steps, and classifier-free guidance scale five. Public actuator position commands are resampled to 60 Hz and normalized by the training set’s first and 99th percentiles for each family. Stewart occupies action channels 14–19 and Delta channels 14–16, with zero-based indexing; unused channels are zero-filled and masked in the training loss. The native causal order generates each video chunk before inserting its known planned commands into the action cache for subsequent chunks. Generation seeds are paired by training-seed/test-case identity across checkpoints. The three zero-shot repetitions share the base weights and vary generation randomness; the adapted repetitions additionally vary training randomness. All 1,800 videos are finite, comprising 210,600 generated future frames.

sections.heading: S.1 One continuous score at fixed engineering targets
sections.text: Each criterion reduces a trajectory to its registered nonnegative SI error, which the continuous map s ⁡ ( ρ ) = 100 / ( 1 + ρ 2 ) s(\rho)=100/(1+\rho^{2}) scores using ρ = r / τ \rho=r/\tau . For multiple channels, ρ \rho is the largest channel-wise error-to-tolerance ratio. The primary S comp S_{\rm comp} averages all six contributions over registered trajectories with equal condition, family, and seed weights. Missing measurements contribute zero to this fixed denominator and case count, while their raw physical errors are reported as N/A. The map assigns 100, 50, and 20 points at errors of zero, one, and two tolerances, respectively, capturing improvements such as KeyCLD’s RK4 gains even when strict joint qualification remains zero. Three perfectly satisfied criteria contribute 50 points to the composite, while raw residuals, physical coverage, and the joint rate show which requirements still fail. Native predictions and reconstructed trajectories use the same scoring rule, with their results reported separately to expose the effect of correction. Reconstruction introduces public geometry into saved predictions. In the overview figure, KeyCLD at 256 pixels receives 50.00 points from reconstructed closure and its two differentiated constraints, and 3.10 from effort, energy, and tracking combined. Adapted LingBot receives 48.15 and 4.97 points from these respective groups, with missing cases retained. Their similar totals, 53.10 and 53.12, thus reflect different component profiles on different tasks. The planar and spatial targets normalize each task’s engineering requirements; model comparisons within a task retain the same mechanisms, commands, and targets. Engineering targets describe the task, mechanism, and actuator. They remain fixed across models and input resolutions within a task; spatial effort and work targets use the registered actuator and command scales. Measurement calibration instead describes the camera, reader, derivative estimator, and operating range. We fit instruments on training identities, select processing on development references, and replay correct videos through the same path as generated videos. Reference replay reveals systematic bias and temporal variation. Measurement configurations are compared on identical reference videos and saved forecasts, with forecasting weights held fixed. Reference RMSE is neither subtracted from model RMSE nor used to enlarge engineering targets. For a calibrated horizontal field of view L L , pixel spacing is L / N L/N when L L spans pixel edges, or L / ( N − 1 ) L/(N-1) when it spans first and last pixel centers. The planar corpus uses the latter convention with L = 1.30 L=1.30 m. Pixel spacing converts image positions into meters, whereas localization accuracy depends on the reader and can be subpixel. Coordinate bias, covariance, temporal dependence, and the nonlinear measurement path govern propagation into velocity, acceleration, effort, and work. Hard geometric constraints independently determine rod-length preservation.

sections.heading: Two sources of uncertainty.
sections.text: Seed/assembly bootstrap intervals describe variation in model results under a fixed measurement path, while calibration quantiles characterize that path’s reference errors. sections.heading: S.3 Numerical differentiation and sensitivity controls
sections.text: Exact sampled trajectories isolate differentiation from visual localization. On 54 independent 30 Hz references, a seven-frame cubic Savitzky–Golay estimator passes all six criteria on 40/54 trajectories. A quintic interpolating spline passes 54/54 on the same trajectories. Worst-case velocity and acceleration constraint errors fall from 0.0219 0.0219 m/s and 2.119 2.119 m/s 2 to 0.000281 0.000281 m/s and 0.0249 0.0249 m/s 2 . Its worst-case torque and energy errors are 0.00298 0.00298 N m and 0.01291 0.01291 J. A 5 mm radial displacement, 0.8 × 0.8\times time scaling, and a 0.5 0.5 N m force offset remain detectable in all 54 controls. Differentiating image-derived coordinates also amplifies localization noise. For the geometric intervention only, we fit crank phase locally and reconstruct derivatives analytically on the manifold. We select window length and polynomial degree by development position, velocity, and acceleration error, subject to all 54 exact-state development trajectories still passing. This selects a seven-frame cubic phase estimator; a 21-frame cubic fit lowers image-derived residuals but fails the exact-state preservation requirement. Native point and closure errors are computed before this intervention. On the 27 clean verification clips, the phase estimator reduces mean reference-image torque error from 1.94 to 0.74 N m and energy error from 2.25 to 0.51 J. It preserves 54/54 exact-state passes and detects the time-scaling, 1 Hz phase, and force-offset controls. Its acceleration gain falls from 0.965 at 1 Hz to 0.720 at 3 Hz, motivating joint reporting with the unfiltered coordinate diagnostic. We introduce a framework for measuring and diagnosing mechanical consistency in visual dynamics. An independent SI audit of rigid closed chains separates geometric admissibility, reaction-free actuator effort, and work–energy balance. Continuous scoring measures progress against fixed engineering targets, while reference replay quantifies measurement error. With three seeds per setting, we evaluate KeyCLD and CON across 343 planar assemblies at 64 / 256 64/256 pixels and V-JEPA + AC and LingBot-VA on 100 shared spatial test assemblies. CON reduces image MSE by 37.6 % / 37.2 % 37.6\%/37.2\% relative to persistence, yet neither planar model attains valid native geometry. At 256 pixels, calibrated RGB replay places forecast errors far above measurement error. With exact states, KeyCLD preserves geometry and RK4 training raises its score from 52.65 to 64.30. In both spatial pathways, CAD/IK reconstruction restores geometry while mean actuator residuals exceed five times the engineering targets. The interventions distinguish gains in visual prediction and geometric admissibility from remaining force and energy errors. 1 Introduction Picking objects, folding garments, and opening doors require predictions that support physical interaction. We study mechanical consistency: agreement between predicted motion and independently specified geometry, forces, and work in SI units. Evaluating these relations connects visual prediction to the actuator demands of physical interaction. Rigid closed chains make these relations concrete. Their closure constraints define admissible configurations, while speed and acceleration along the same path determine different actuator demands. A prediction can therefore trace a valid shape and still require the wrong torque, providing a controlled setting for diagnosing mechanical consistency. Our independent SI audit first checks the predicted configuration, then eliminates unknown joint reactions to evaluate actuator effort and work–energy balance ( Fig. 1 ). Reference replay and targeted interventions locate errors in coordinate readout, numerical integration, and the learned force model. Figure 1 : Four pathways from pixels to mechanics. (a) After reconstruction, blue/tan bars show measurable/unavailable fractions, with measurable/total counts and percentages. Effort/energy plots show cases, quartiles, ranges, and dashed tolerances. Below, six contributions sum to S comp S_{\rm comp} ; arrows show reconstruction gains and 50 marks the maximum kinematic contribution. Scores use task-specific targets with balanced seeds, families, and conditions; each spatial pathway contains 900 cases (LingBot FT: 50 updates). (b,c) Physical readouts feed kinematic and effort/energy tests using independent SI parameters ( B ​ u A = e 1 ​ τ A Bu_{A}=e_{1}\tau_{A} for planar chains). We apply the audit to constrained Lagrangian dynamics (KeyCLD) [ 4 ] and latent coupled oscillators (CON) [ 13 ] at two planar image resolutions, then to predictive features (V-JEPA 2.1 + AC) [ 12 , 1 ] and generative video–action modeling (LingBot-VA) [ 10 ] on Stewart and Delta mechanisms. Resolution and measurement controls test whether physical failures persist as visual information and localization accuracy improve. We contribute (1) a six-criterion framework for mechanical consistency and tracking, with continuous SI tolerance scoring; (2) reference calibration and interventions that separate observation, integration, and constitutive effects; and (3) a 343-assembly planar benchmark at two resolutions and a 100-test-assembly spatial study, spanning four modeling paradigms. 2 Related Work Structured mechanical learning. Hamiltonian [ 7 ] and Lagrangian networks [ 3 , 11 ] encode mechanical structure, while Cartesian constraints simplify admissible dynamics [ 5 ] . Analyses of these inductive biases [ 8 ] motivate testing what each structural choice guarantees. Our audit checks whether acceleration along the admissible manifold agrees with independently specified forces and work. Learning physical evolution from images. Hamiltonian Generative Networks [ 15 ] and coordinate-aware Lagrangian models [ 17 ] link images to mechanics. KeyCLD learns constrained keypoints, masses, potential, and actuation [ 4 ] ; CON couples autoencoding to dissipative latent oscillators [ 13 ] . Dissipative SymODEN represents velocity-dependent forces [ 18 ] . V-JEPA 2.1 learns dense predictive features [ 12 ] for action-conditioned latent rollouts [ 1 ] ; LingBot-VA jointly models video and actions by autoregressive diffusion [ 10 ] . We audit their connections to SI states and forces. Physical evaluation. Physion tests visual prediction [ 2 ] , MechVerse evaluates kinematic coupling [ 9 ] , and video benchmarks test physical laws [ 6 ] , including force–motion consistency in GAUGE [ 16 ] .
